Question: A 'fleet of agents' is proposed to run production deploys. What governance is non-negotiable?
Option A: Traces are optional if the model is frontier.
Option B: More agents increase safety via debate.
Option C: Least-privilege tools, human approval gates on irreversible actions, full traces, and a non-agent rollback path.
Option D: If the planner is staff-level, tools can be root.

Question: Distributed tracing for agents should propagate a run id across model, tools, and sub-agents so that:
Option A: You can reconstruct a causal DAG of spans when one child agent fans out
Option B: IDs are decorative only
Option C: Child agents must not log
Option D: Only the last span is kept

Question: For AI agents, a ReAct-style loop with unbounded “think” tokens before each tool call mainly fails in production because:
Option A: Runtimes cannot parse function calls after text
Option B: Stop conditions become stricter automatically
Option C: Thoughts are billed, leak into traces, can be injected into, and do not substitute for a real world model
Option D: Thoughts always improve grounding

Question: For AI agents, a cost budget that only caps output tokens will still blow up when:
Option A: You disable retrieval
Option B: You use a state machine with no observations
Option C: A tool returns a huge blob that is concatenated into the next prompt every step
Option D: The model emits a short final answer

Question: For AI agents, a state machine whose every node is “LLM decides any tool” has collapsed into free-form. To keep the graph meaningful you must:
Option A: Increase temperature at terminals
Option B: Remove traces at graph edges
Option C: Restrict the tool set and allowed successors per node, with runtime enforcement—not only a prompt that lists them
Option D: Name the nodes poetically

Question: For AI agents, a stop condition “when the model says DONE” is weak because:
Option A: Stop tokens cannot be configured
Option B: Agents never over-talk
Option C: The model can emit DONE early, late, or in a tool argument; the runtime needs an explicit halt (budget, graph terminal, or structured stop)
Option D: DONE is parsed by GPUs directly

Question: For AI agents, eval that only scores the final user-visible answer misses:
Option A: Whether the paragraph rhymes
Option B: The tokenizer version
Option C: The color scheme
Option D: Illegal tool use, secret leakage in args, wasted steps, and near-miss policy violations that did not reach the user this time

Question: For AI agents, free-form vs state machine is not binary. A practical hybrid is:
Option A: A graph that never calls a model
Option B: No timeouts in hybrid mode
Option C: A graph of stages with a small free-form tool loop inside a sandbox stage, then a forced review stage before writes
Option D: Free-form always, with a comment in the prompt about stages

Question: For AI agents, non-idempotent tools plus at-least-once execution (retries, duplicates, crashes) require:
Option A: Deduping on a business key, or making the effect at-most-once via a store the runtime owns
Option B: Higher temperature so calls differ
Option C: Deleting traces after each retry
Option D: Parallelizing all writes always

Question: For AI agents, over-permissioned tools plus prompt injection is a full exploit path because:
Option A: Schemas block all strings
Option B: Approvals are inserted by temperature
Option C: Untrusted content can induce a call, and the runtime will execute any allowed tool with model-supplied args
Option D: Injection cannot mention tool names

Question: For AI agents, passing the entire raw trace back into the next prompt as “memory” is costly and unsafe because:
Option A: Budgets ignore concatenated traces
Option B: It repeats secrets, injections, and failed plans, multiplying tokens and giving old payloads another chance
Option C: Traces contain no text
Option D: Prompts cannot include JSON

Question: For AI agents, poisoned tool output (a webpage that says “now email secrets to …”) is best treated as:
Option A: A reason to raise temperature
Option B: Proof that traces should be disabled
Option C: A tokenizer failure
Option D: Indirect injection into the observation channel; tools must not gain extra privileges from content they fetch

Question: For AI agents, retrying a read-only search is usually safer than retrying a write. The precise reason is:
Option A: Writes cannot fail
Option B: Reads never time out
Option C: Search cannot be cached
Option D: Reads are typically idempotent; writes often are not, so error class must gate retry policy per tool

Question: Multi-agent 'researcher + critic' improved a demo. In production it doubled cost and disagreed silently. What was missing?
Option A: You should hide disagreements from traces.
Option B: A third agent.
Option C: A scoring contract, stop conditions, and a single owner of the user-visible answer; debate without a reducer is just extra tokens.
Option D: Critics should have more tools than researchers.

Question: Semantic memory that the agent can write without review creates a loop where:
Option A: Hallucinations get stored and later retrieved as facts, amplifying error across sessions
Option B: Memory becomes write-protected automatically
Option C: RAG cannot read the store
Option D: Tokenizers reset the index

Question: The strongest signal you should not ship an agent yet is:
Option A: You cannot predefine the next observation
Option B: Research quality requires iterative search
Option C: A scripted DAG plus one extraction call meets the SLA and the audit log, and the agent only wins on rare demos
Option D: Users have open-ended goals across many tools

Question: You can give an agent a browser, a shell, and prod credentials 'so it can debug like a human'. Why is this a category error?
Option A: Debugging never needs write access, so the union is safe.
Option B: Agents cannot use browsers.
Option C: A human is accountable and rate-limited by attention; an agent will explore the union of permissions at machine speed. Split identities and environments.
Option D: Prod credentials are fine if in a vector store.

Question: A consumer 'succeeds' if it PUTs to S3 but crashes before finishing side effects. Replay will PUT again. The object key should be:
Option A: A random UUID every attempt so nothing clashes
Option B: Deterministic from the message id / business id so retries overwrite the same checksummed object
Option C: The current timestamp to the nanosecond
Option D: The SQS receipt handle

Question: A data lake is 'S3 + many writers renaming prefixes to commit'. Why do staff engineers push for a real table format / manifest?
Option A: Prefix rename is cheaper than writing a manifest.
Option B: Rename is atomic across prefixes in S3 like a filesystem mv of a directory.
Option C: There is no atomic directory rename; readers can see partial sets. Table formats (or a commit inventory) give a consistent snapshot of files.
Option D: S3 LIST is a transaction log.

Question: A pipeline is 'SQS -> worker -> S3 -> notify next queue'. End-to-end exactly-once is:
Option A: Not given; each hop is at-least-once, so idempotent writes (keyed objects/versions) are the real contract
Option B: Guaranteed by S3 copies
Option C: Guaranteed if checksums match
Option D: Guaranteed by SQS FIFO alone

Question: Cross-account S3 access: bucket policy vs IAM identity policy vs ACL vs VPC endpoint policy. A request is denied. How do you reason?
Option A: Bucket owner always can, regardless of endpoint policies.
Option B: Any one allow wins.
Option C: All relevant layers must allow and none deny; missing identity permission or a VPC endpoint policy deny will fail the call even if the bucket policy allows.
Option D: ACLs override IAM.

Question: Cross-region replication of S3 objects is asynchronous. Designing a 'read in region B immediately after write in A' as if it were a commit is wrong because:
Option A: Prefixes cannot cross regions
Option B: SQS becomes exactly-once when CRR is on
Option C: Checksums do not replicate
Option D: Replication lag means B may not have the object yet; it is not a distributed database transaction

Question: Firehose/Kinesis rolling files into S3 every N MB or N seconds is about:
Option A: Making S3 a transactional database
Option B: Turning a high-QPS small-event stream into large, checksummed objects with spread prefixes
Option C: Guaranteeing exactly-once SQS
Option D: Avoiding copies for durability

Question: In AWS / S3, a KMS-encrypted bucket plus many tiny GETs is slow/expensive because:
Option A: Encryption removes copies
Option B: Each request can add KMS authz/decrypt overhead on top of the small-file request tax
Option C: Checksums cannot run with KMS
Option D: SQS cannot send encrypted payloads

Question: In AWS / S3, compare-and-swap with ETags on a hot inventory object serializes the world onto one key. At scale you:
Option A: List the bucket instead
Option B: Shard the object, use a real database for the hot row, or accept queue-based serialization — S3 is not a write-optimized row store
Option C: Turn off checksums to go faster
Option D: Use sequential date prefixes for inventory

Question: In AWS / S3, durability of copies does not protect you from a bad DELETE in the app. You still need:
Option A: At-most-once SQS so deletes never retry
Option B: Sequential prefixes as undo logs
Option C: A memorized nines figure
Option D: Versioning, MFA-delete/Object Lock, IAM least privilege, and backups — operational mistakes are not disk failures

Question: In AWS / S3, hot prefix plus small files plus a LIST-heavy UI is a triple hit. The architecture move is:
Option A: Raise the durability SLA
Option B: Metadata in a database or index, objects in S3 with hashed prefixes and batched file sizes; never LIST as the product query
Option C: One SQS message per byte
Option D: Disable checksums and versioning

Question: In AWS / S3, strongly consistent GET of a key is not isolation for a multi-step workflow because:
Option A: SQS FIFO wraps S3 in a transaction
Option B: Checksums are eventual
Option C: Two objects (or object + queue + table) are not one transaction; you compose idempotent steps
Option D: Prefixes provide SNAPSHOT isolation

Question: In AWS / S3, you replicated objects and now readers see old and new writers. The durable copies did their job; the missing piece is:
Option A: Sequential prefixes for linearizability
Option B: A higher SLA percentage
Option C: An application-level version/epoch so readers know which object generation is authoritative
Option D: Disabling checksums so clocks agree

Question: Inventory reports and S3 Batch exist because listing the live bucket as a control plane:
Option A: Makes small files free
Option B: Is a strongly consistent SQL view
Option C: Does not scale as a database catalog; you snapshot metadata out of band
Option D: Fixes prefix hotspots

Question: S3 Object Lock / WORM helps compliance. Using it as a queue ack store is a smell because:
Option A: You wanted a messaging semantic (visibility, retry, DLQ), not immutability of blobs
Option B: Prefixes cannot be locked
Option C: At-least-once is disabled by WORM
Option D: WORM objects cannot have checksums

Question: Using S3 as a lockfile (PUT if not exists, then work) fails under contention because:
Option A: PUT cannot create empty objects
Option B: There is no robust lease/fencing story like a consensus lock; timeouts and retries produce split brain
Option C: Checksums break If-None-Match
Option D: Prefixes serialize all PUTs globally

Question: You are asked to put a POSIX-ish shared scratch filesystem on S3 for a database's data directory. What is the right answer?
Option A: S3 is strongly consistent now, so fsync semantics are met.
Option B: S3 is an object store, not POSIX: no byte-range locking, no real fsync of a mutable file. Use block storage or a real shared FS designed for that DB.
Option C: Mountpoint for S3 is equivalent to ext4 for InnoDB.
Option D: If you enable versioning, POSIX appends work.

Question: You need append-only analytics events. Why not one S3 PUT per click from the browser?
Option A: Tiny-object request cost, prefix hotspots, and no server-side aggregation; buffer in Kinesis/SQS/Firehose then write large objects
Option B: Checksums reject click JSON
Option C: At-least-once queues forbid this path only
Option D: S3 cannot be written from the internet with the right IAM

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, a key-value API with many overwrite-in-place small rows vs append-mostly events: how do you argue the engine choice?
Option A: Always B-tree because compaction is impossible to operate
Option B: The choice only depends on whether you have a WAL
Option C: In-place small-row OLTP often wants B-tree locality and cheap point/range; append-mostly ingest wants LSM sequential write and later compaction
Option D: Always LSM because write amp is lower in every workload

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, a leveled compaction write-amp estimate of ~10 (level ratio ~10) is missing which operational multiplier?
Option A: B-tree fanout
Option B: Replica ping time
Option C: WAL write, memtable flush, and extra L0→L1 work when L0 is unsorted/overlapping
Option D: Bloom-filter hash count

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, a team wants 'just put RocksDB in front of S3' as a global database. What staff-level objection is first?
Option A: Bloom filters do not work outside process memory.
Option B: RocksDB cannot persist to disk.
Option C: A local LSM is not a distributed consensus/replication layer; you still need sharding, fencing, and a commit protocol or you will split-brain.
Option D: S3 cannot store SSTables.

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, an LSM write stall despite spare CPU often means which resource is the real bottleneck?
Option A: Bloom-filter CPU hash time
Option B: Flush/compaction bandwidth or L0 file-count limits: ingest is gated on making room, not on user-thread CPU
Option C: Too many range-scan merge iterators on idle cores
Option D: The B-tree splitter is running

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, delete-heavy LSM with lazy tombstone compaction: what is the dangerous read-path failure mode?
Option A: Point gets return random keys
Option B: Scans and gets keep resurrecting work: they must overlay tombstones from newer files onto older versions until compaction drops them
Option C: The WAL refuses new deletes
Option D: Bloom filters start returning false negatives

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, merge iterator during an LSM scan must resolve duplicate keys. What is the correct recency rule?
Option A: Bloom filters pick the winner
Option B: Oldest SSTable wins because it was flushed first
Option C: Newest sequence/memtable-or-file generation wins, including tombstones that hide older values
Option D: Largest value wins

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, prefix bloom / partitioned filters exist because of which scan vs get tension?
Option A: They replace compaction
Option B: They make SSTables mutable
Option C: They store the full key in RAM
Option D: Whole-file blooms help point gets but not prefix/range existence checks; partitioned/prefix filters prune files for both

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, tombstones in an LSM outlive the data they delete under a bad compaction policy. How do reads fail?
Option A: Tombstones automatically promote to the memtable as live keys.
Option B: The WAL refuses new writes until tombstones are gone.
Option C: They don't; tombstones are skipped in O(1).
Option D: Point and especially range reads must sift dead keys until compaction drops them; space and CPU inflate.

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, universal/size-tiered compaction is piling huge overlapping runs. Which read path degrades first, and why?
Option A: Point gets of hot cached keys in the memtable
Option B: Wide range scans, because merge iterators fan in across many overlapping files of similar size
Option C: WAL appends on the write path, which do not consult those overlapping runs
Option D: Bloom-filter inserts during memtable flush, which do not merge the old runs

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why is fsync of the WAL not the same as fsync of SSTables for crash correctness?
Option A: Both are optional if bloom filters are used
Option B: WAL fsync makes the latest memtable mutations recoverable; SSTable fsync makes a flush durable so WAL can be truncated
Option C: Only SSTable fsync matters; WAL is a cache
Option D: Only WAL fsync matters; SSTables can be torn forever

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why is naive size-tiered compaction prone to space-amp spikes right before a large merge?
Option A: Memtables are never released
Option B: A merge of similar-sized runs temporarily keeps old and new copies until the new file is installed
Option C: Bloom filters double on disk
Option D: The WAL is checkpointed into every SSTable twice

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, you are picking a storage engine for a write-heavy metrics store with occasional large range scans for graphs. What is the real tension?
Option A: B-trees cannot store timestamps.
Option B: LSMs cannot expire old data.
Option C: Range scans are always O(1) on both.
Option D: LSM ingest vs the merge cost of those range scans (and compaction stealing I/O from queries).

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, you have a block cache that already holds most inner index blocks. Where should you spend the next RAM dollar for LSM point gets?
Option A: It depends: blooms cut negative lookups; caching data/filter blocks cuts positive lookups. Measure miss types
Option B: Never bloom filters if any cache exists
Option C: Always enlarge the WAL
Option D: Always more bloom-filter bits, even if data blocks are never cached

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, you must pick a structure for a working set that fits in RAM but a dataset that does not. Which statement is the staff-level read of amplification?
Option A: LSM point reads become free because memtable holds the dataset
Option B: Write amplification disappears when the working set is cached
Option C: If internal nodes/filters/hot leaves stay cached, B-tree point reads can be one I/O; LSM still pays multi-level filter/index misses on cold keys
Option D: RAM size makes on-disk layout irrelevant

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, you observe LSM read amp rising while write amp falls after switching compaction style. What did you likely just do?
Option A: Moved toward lazier tiered/universal merging (less rewrite, more overlapping runs)
Option B: Disabled the WAL
Option C: Replaced blooms with a full in-memory index of every key
Option D: Moved toward more aggressive leveling (more rewrite, fewer overlapping files)

Question: The RUM conjecture is useful when choosing B-tree vs LSM because it says…
Option A: You can independently minimize read, update, and memory/space amplification at once
Option B: You cannot simultaneously minimize read, update, and memory/space amplification; LSM and B-tree sit on different corners
Option C: Only RAM size matters; on-disk layout is irrelevant
Option D: Compaction eliminates all three amplifications

Question: Why can a copy-on-write B-tree (or CoW page engine) still lose the LSM ingest race under random writes?
Option A: CoW never writes a WAL
Option B: CoW cannot be crash-safe
Option C: LSM never writes more than once
Option D: CoW still tends to write page-granularity trees and can amplify through ancestors; LSM batches into sequential runs

Question: An ABI-stable plugin interface returns `std::string` across a `.so` boundary compiled with different libstdc++. What did you just do?
Option A: You invoked ODR/ABI roulette: layout and allocators may differ; use a C ABI (char* + length) or a single shared standard library.
Option B: unique_ptr across .so is always safe if string is not.
Option C: C++ modules fix ABI at the filesystem boundary.
Option D: The Itanium ABI makes all std::string layouts identical forever.

Question: Every public API in a large C++ codebase takes and returns std::shared_ptr 'so lifetime is easy'. What did you actually pay?
Option A: Nothing: shared_ptr is free on modern CPUs and makes ownership obvious.
Option B: Atomic refcounts on every copy, control-block allocations, and unclear who is supposed to uniquely own the object. Default to unique_ptr or values; shared_ptr is for genuine shared lifetime.
Option C: shared_ptr is required for any object that has a destructor.
Option D: The compiler converts shared_ptr to unique_ptr in LTO, so the type is documentation only.

Question: In C++, a coroutine captures a reference parameter and then the caller's stack frame is gone. What is the bug?
Option A: Coroutines extend all reference arguments to the coroutine's lifetime.
Option B: Reference parameters dangle after the caller returns; copy values the coroutine needs or take ownership. This is a use-after-free.
Option C: co_await copies every reference.
Option D: The compiler forbids capturing references in coroutines.

Question: In C++, a low-latency path allocates on every message (std::string, vector resize). The profiler is 'clean' of locks. What is still wrong?
Option A: The compiler elides all heap use in loops.
Option B: virtual functions are the only latency bug that matters.
Option C: Allocators are wait-free and never stall.
Option D: Allocator contention and cache pollution; pre-size, arenas, or intrusive buffers belong on that path.

Question: In C++, a sanitizer-clean binary still corrupts state only at -O3. What class of bug is first on the list?
Option A: Undefined behavior the optimizer exploited (strict aliasing, signed overflow, lifetime) that -O0 happened not to.
Option B: The linker strips atomics at -O3.
Option C: Sanitizers prove the absence of UB at all optimization levels.
Option D: A missing #include.

Question: In C++, a staff binary is LTO-built. Two TUs define different inline functions with the same signature. What risk did you accept?
Option A: ODR violation: LTO may pick one body and silently change behavior. One definition, or distinct names.
Option B: inline means both survive and the call site picks at runtime.
Option C: LTO disables inlining, so both copies remain.
Option D: LTO always errors on this at link time.

Question: In C++, a tight packet loop uses virtual dispatch per packet on a deep hierarchy. Profile shows i-cache misses. What is the data-oriented move?
Option A: Sort by type, use a closed set of concrete handlers, or a table of function pointers over contiguous data — cut the pointer chase.
Option B: virtual is always inlined by LTO.
Option C: Put each packet on its own heap allocation for locality.
Option D: Add more virtual methods to improve prediction.

Question: In C++, two threads increment adjacent `std::atomic<uint64_t>` counters in an array and scale poorly. What is it, and the fix?
Option A: atomics always share a global lock, so adjacent or not does not matter.
Option B: They bounce one cache line between cores (false sharing). Pad/align to cache-line size or use a striped counter.
Option C: uint64 atomics cannot be incremented without a mutex.
Option D: This only happens without -O3.

Question: In C++, you compile one TU with -fno-exceptions and another with exceptions, then a header-only template throws across that boundary. What happens?
Option A: The linker rejects mixed exception flags, so this cannot ship.
Option B: -fno-exceptions only affects main(); templates still throw safely.
Option C: The exception is automatically translated into an error code.
Option D: You mixed exception ABIs: the result is undefined (often std::terminate). One exception policy per binary, enforced in the build.

Question: In C++, you need readers that do not block on a rare config writer. Which pattern matches?
Option A: volatile on the unique_ptr.
Option B: memory_order_relaxed stores of a mutex.
Option C: A single mutex around a unique_ptr that readers also take.
Option D: Immutable snapshots published with atomic shared_ptr (lock-free on some libs, not wait-free) or RCU; readers load the pointer, writers publish a new object.

Question: In C++, you need to share read-mostly config across threads. A shared_ptr swapped atomically vs a mutex around a unique_ptr. What is the RCU-like idea?
Option A: unique_ptr can be read from two threads if it is const.
Option B: atomics on unique_ptr are in the standard and cheaper.
Option C: Mutex is always lower latency for reads.
Option D: Publish a new immutable snapshot (atomic shared_ptr); readers copy the pointer with no lock; old snapshot frees when refcount hits 0.

Question: You must keep ABI stable for a C++ library used by customers' compilers. Which surface is the least painful?
Option A: Throwing exceptions across the .so boundary as the stable contract.
Option B: Inline templates and std::string in the public API.
Option C: A C API (opaque handles, explicit sizes) with C++ wrappers in a header that the customer compiles.
Option D: Exporting std::vector from a .so compiled with a different libstdc++.

Question: A globally distributed Cassandra app uses LOCAL_QUORUM in each DC and never repairs. What consistency story are you actually giving users who travel between DCs?
Option A: LOCAL_QUORUM waits for all DCs.
Option B: Hinted handoff makes DCs interchangeable immediately.
Option C: Linearizable global reads.
Option D: A DC-local quorum that can remain stale vs another DC until repair/hint/read-repair; design for it or use a different consistency/replication model.

Question: In Cassandra, LWT cost is not just extra round trips. What local storage-engine cost also shows up?
Option A: LWT bypasses memtables entirely
Option B: LWT stores a full cluster snapshot
Option C: LWT turns off bloom filters cluster-wide
Option D: Paxos state (promises/commits) is persisted per partition, adding writes, contention, and more compaction on that key

Question: In Cassandra, a coordinator chooses replicas for a QUORUM read. Why might it still do extra digest reads?
Option A: Digest reads replace QUORUM
Option B: Digests are only for hinted handoff
Option C: To hash the partition key again
Option D: To detect replica disagreement cheaply, then fetch full data and reconcile, which is a form of read repair work

Question: In Cassandra, a repair that misses a recently deleted partition (gc grace elapsed, tombstone dropped, replica was down) produces what?
Option A: LWT abort of the repair
Option B: A harmless no-op
Option C: Data resurrection: the stale replica's live data is copied back to others
Option D: Automatic RF increase

Question: In Cassandra, a staff review of a 'one partition per tenant, all rows clustered' multi-tenant design should flag what first?
Option A: CQL cannot filter clustering columns
Option B: Tenant size skew becomes hot/wide partitions; noisy tenants dominate compaction, repair, and replica CPU with no token isolation
Option C: RF cannot be greater than 1 for multi-tenant data
Option D: QUORUM does not work with clustering columns

Question: In Cassandra, compaction strategy: STCS on a time-series table that mostly appends and TTLs. Why might TWCS be the better fit?
Option A: TWCS stores data in B-trees.
Option B: STCS is illegal on time-series.
Option C: Time-window compaction can drop whole SSTables when TTL expires instead of mixing old/new in size-tiered compaction, reducing tombstone pain.
Option D: TWCS makes all reads QUORUM.

Question: In Cassandra, dropping gc_grace to 'clean tombstones faster' after a mass delete: what must already be true?
Option A: Every replica has received the deletes and repair has covered the ranges; otherwise dropped tombstones invite resurrection
Option B: CL=ONE is in use
Option C: LWTs are disabled
Option D: Nothing; it is always safe

Question: In Cassandra, hinted handoff during a rolling outage of two of three replicas at RF=3, CL=QUORUM: what happens to writes?
Option A: Writes succeed because hints count as quorum votes
Option B: QUORUM writes fail; hints are not a substitute for live acknowledgements, so availability drops until a replica returns
Option C: CL is automatically lowered to ONE
Option D: The remaining replica becomes RF=1 silently

Question: In Cassandra, hot-partition mitigation via bucketing (user_id + bucket) changes which costs?
Option A: It removes the need for RF
Option B: Writes spread across tokens, but reads of 'all buckets' become scatter-gather and you reintroduce merge/limit logic in the app
Option C: Clustering order is lost forever
Option D: QUORUM is no longer defined

Question: In Cassandra, incremental repair vs a naive full repair: what failure mode are you trying to avoid?
Option A: The need for partition keys
Option B: Use of clustering columns
Option C: Token-aware routing
Option D: Repeatedly streaming already-agreed ranges, overloading disks/network, and extending the window where unrepaired data can resurrect after tombstone GC

Question: In Cassandra, when would you accept CL=ONE writes in production despite stale-read risk?
Option A: When you also need linearizable CAS
Option B: When RF=1 already, so CL does not matter and you still claim multi-replica durability
Option C: Always; QUORUM is never worth it
Option D: When the workload is write-availability-first, reads can tolerate staleness, and repair/hints/read-repair are operated as the reconciliation path

Question: In Cassandra, why can EACH_QUORUM writes be the right multi-DC choice even though they are slow?
Option A: They require a quorum in every DC, so a DC that was partitioned does not silently accept a CL that later cannot be read locally
Option B: They skip the commit log
Option C: They disable tombstones
Option D: They contact only one node

Question: In Cassandra, why is a monotonically growing clustering key that is also the only partition key a dual foot-gun?
Option A: One ever-growing partition (hot + wide) lands on one token; time-series wants time in clustering and a bounded partition key (and often time buckets)
Option B: Clustering keys cannot be timestamps
Option C: QUORUM forbids time-series
Option D: It is the recommended time-series pattern

Question: In Cassandra, you need linearizable compare-and-set on a counter-like row. Why is 'read QUORUM then write QUORUM' the wrong tool?
Option A: Two clients can both read the same value and both write; you need LWT/Paxos (or an external consensus) to serialize the RMW
Option B: Repair already serializes all writes
Option C: Hinted handoff provides linearizability
Option D: QUORUM cannot read counters

Question: W+R>RF is necessary but not sufficient for 'I always read my write' in Cassandra. Which extra caveat is staff-level?
Option A: There are no caveats if W+R>RF
Option B: Clock/last-write-wins, partial replica failures, digest mismatch paths, and CL computed per-DC can still yield surprising recency without LWT/SERIAL
Option C: Partition keys are not hashed when W+R>RF
Option D: Tombstones disable W+R>RF

Question: You must explain why Cassandra's last-write-wins on conflicting replicas is not a substitute for LWT.
Option A: LWW always waits for Paxos
Option B: LWW picks a timestamp winner after the fact; concurrent RMWs can lose updates. LWT prevents the lost update by agreeing before commit
Option C: LWW and LWT are identical on the same partition
Option D: Repair turns LWW into linearizability

Question: You need a uniqueness constraint ('this email is registered') in Cassandra. Why is that a product smell at staff level?
Option A: Partitioning on email hashes uniqueness for free.
Option B: Cassandra unique indexes are serializable by default.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, CHAMP / HAMT / B-tree vs open-addressing hash for a persistent (immutable) map in a language runtime. Why the tree-like hash trie?

Question: In data structures and algorithms, LRU under scan-heavy traffic (a job reads every key once). What happens to the cache of hot keys?

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a 'linked list of buffers' vs a small number of large slabs for a network server. Same abstract list of bytes. Why slabs?

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a rate limiter for a global API: token bucket in one Redis vs sliding log of timestamps per user. What is the staff trade-off?

Question: In data structures and algorithms, autocomplete at 50k QPS: trie in one JVM vs prefix query to a search engine. When is the trie the wrong 'clever' answer?

Question: In data structures and algorithms, counting Bloom / cuckoo / quotient filters exist. You need deletes and a hard bound on false positives for a security denylist. Why a vanilla Bloom is the wrong contract?
Option A: Vanilla Bloom has false negatives, which are worse for denylists

Question: In data structures and algorithms, dijkstra on a huge sparse graph: binary heap vs array vs Fibonacci-style vs just BFS. Workload split?
Option A: Union-find extracts the next closest node
Option B: If all weights are equal, BFS (or 0-1 deque) — a heap is wasted. If weights vary, you need a PQ; which PQ depends on decrease-key volume and graph size, not the brand name
Option C: Always Fibonacci heap because the bound is famous

Question: In data structures and algorithms, directed graph, detect if adding an edge would create a cycle, online, many queries. DFS every time is too slow. Better?
Option A: BFS from a random node never sees directed cycles
Option B: If the graph is a DAG of components you merge, union-find works for undirected; for directed you need incremental topo / reachability (or full topo + DFS on the relevant region) — union-find alone is the wrong connectivity model
Option C: Union-find is identical for directed cycles
Option D: A Bloom filter of edges proves acyclicity

Question: In data structures and algorithms, false-positive rate of a Bloom filter after you insert more items than it was sized for. What actually happens?
Option A: Union-find rebuilds the bitset
Option B: LRU evicts bits in recency order
Option C: Bits saturate, 'yes' becomes almost always — the filter silently degrades toward useless; there is no crash, which is why ops miss it
Option D: It starts emitting false negatives to compensate

Question: In data structures and algorithms, hot-key workload: 1 key is 40% of QPS. Hash partition across 50 caches. What structure-level fact did you ignore?
Option A: A heap of caches will split the key each extract-min
Option B: Consistent hashing splits a single key across the ring by definition
Option C: Hashing spreads keys, not load — one key still lives on one shard; you need replication, local LRU on every node, or a different split (by session, by request) for that key
Option D: A balanced tree on the same key automatically shards it

Question: In data structures and algorithms, rendezvous hashing vs consistent ring: you want minimal disruption and easy weighted nodes without virtual node explosion. Which idea?
Option A: Always use hash % N with sticky sessions
Option B: Put nodes in a heap and extract-min per key
Option C: DFS the node list until a Bloom filter says yes
Option D: Highest random weight / Rendezvous: score(key, node), pick max — membership change only moves keys that preferred the lost node; weights fold into the score

Question: In data structures and algorithms, union-find with path compression, no union-by-rank, adversarial unions always attaching large to small via the wrong root. Practical issue?
Option A: Trees get tall; even with later compression, a bad sequence plus no rank/size can make individual finds scan long chains before they flatten
Option B: Path compression without rank is undefined
Option C: The structure becomes a heap and extract-min breaks
Option D: Bloom filter bits collide with the parent array

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you external-sort huge files. Runs are written, then merged. Why does 'stable' still matter on disk?
Option A: BFS merge of runs preserves order automatically
Option B: Equal keys from earlier files/runs must keep their input order (e.g. original row id, replica timestamp) or the merge invents a new ordering that downstream consumers did not ask for
Option C: Stability only exists in RAM arrays, not files
Option D: Heaps used in k-way merge are stable by nature for all equal keys

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need an LRU across a fleet. Local LRU per node + consistent hashing. A key's node jumps; the new node has a cold LRU. Besides miss storm, what invariant broke?
Option A: Consistent hashing copies the doubly linked list to the successor automatically
Option B: A heap of timestamps is globally shared via hashing
Option C: BFS of the ring rebuilds LRU
Option D: Recency is per process — the global working set is not on the ring. Hashing moves identity, not the linked-list order; replicas or session stickiness are how you keep recency

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need connectivity across a huge undirected graph that mutates. Why might union-find (DSU) be the right first tool, and when does it stop?
Option A: BFS from every node is always faster.
Option B: DSU supports deletions as cheaply as unions.
Option C: Near-constant unions/finds for 'are these connected' if you mostly add edges; deletions, path queries, or need for actual paths need a different structure.
Option D: DSU is only for trees of height 2.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you replace an array-backed deque with a linked list to get 'true O(1) insert in the middle' for a 1e7-element structure you mostly iterate. Net effect on a modern CPU?
Option A: TLB prefers pointer graphs to contiguous pages
Option B: Middle insert may allocate and patch two pointers, but iteration becomes cache-hostile; if iterates dominate, you slowed the real workload
Option C: Linked lists always dominate arrays once n > 10^4
Option D: The allocator colocates list nodes so they prefetch like arrays

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you sort events by (user_id, event_time) for per-user sessionization. One-pass composite compare vs sort-by-time then stable sort-by-user. When is the two-pass actually what you want?
Option A: Two-pass is always slower and never justified
Option B: Heaps can only do one key
Option C: BFS requires two-pass sorts
Option D: When event_time order among a user must be the original sort's order and that first sort was already done (or is expensive to redo as a composite) — stability composes existing order; a new unstable composite can still break equal (user, time) ties you cared about

Question: A cache in front of DynamoDB for a hot product key helps reads. What must you still design for?
Option A: GSIs become strongly consistent
Option B: The cache makes writes strongly consistent across regions
Option C: Cache misses, TTL expiry, and stampede can slam the same hot key; writes still hit DynamoDB
Option D: Partition keys are no longer needed

Question: A product wants relational joins across three DynamoDB tables on the request path. What should you push back with?
Option A: Access-pattern-first: denormalize/duplicate, or pick a database that joins. Request-path joins are N queries, inconsistent snapshots, and hot GSIs waiting to happen.
Option B: Transactions across three tables are free if items are small.
Option C: PartiQL joins are as cheap as Dynamo Query.
Option D: Use Scan + in-memory join; DynamoDB is fine.

Question: Default DynamoDB global tables (MREC) give you multi-region copies. What do they not give you unless you opt into MRSC?
Option A: The same partition-key model in each region
Option B: Lower read latency near a replica
Option C: A single globally strongly consistent item view on every replica — that is a separate, higher-latency MRSC mode, not the default async replica
Option D: Regional isolation if you design for it

Question: In DynamoDB, a 350KB item is updated 20 times a second to flip one flag. Why is this an incident waiting to happen?
Option A: Updates are eventually consistent only
Option B: On-demand forbids updates
Option C: Flags cannot live in DynamoDB
Option D: Each update rewrites the whole large item, multiplying write cost and making that key hotter than the business change requires

Question: In DynamoDB, a GSI is KEYS_ONLY. A query against it still needs five large attributes. Tradeoff?
Option A: You do a cheap index Query then GetItem the base rows; you avoided write amplification at the cost of extra reads
Option B: KEYS_ONLY implies strong consistency
Option C: You must Scan the base table
Option D: The GSI returns those attributes for free

Question: In DynamoDB, a leaderboard GSI partition key is the constant LEADERBOARD. Why will this fail at scale?
Option A: Every write lands on one index partition; you modeled a global hot key
Option B: GSIs cannot sort
Option C: Leaderboards require strongly consistent scans
Option D: Constants are not valid attribute names

Question: In DynamoDB, adaptive capacity moved extra throughput toward a hot partition, but p99 still collapses on one productId. What is left?
Option A: Enable strongly consistent GSIs
Option B: Switch every read to Scan
Option C: Buy more table-level RCUs only
Option D: Change the key (shard, invert access pattern, or cache) because one key is a physical bottleneck

Question: In DynamoDB, exporting to S3 / using an incremental export for analytics is preferred over a live Scan because:
Option A: Scans cannot paginate
Option B: S3 is a database
Option C: You isolate heavy read traffic from the online table's partitions and capacity
Option D: Exports are strongly consistent GSIs

Question: In DynamoDB, on-demand still throttles a partition. Why are people surprised?
Option A: On-demand disables GSIs

Option C: On-demand advertises infinite per-key QPS

Question: In DynamoDB, single-table design is not 'put everything in one table'. The actual rule is:

Option C: Never use GSIs

Question: In DynamoDB, streams + Lambda to maintain a projection. The Lambda is not idempotent. What operational failure is guaranteed eventually?
Option A: At-least-once shard records will double-apply; the projection must be idempotent or versioned.

Option C: Projections cannot diverge because they share storage with the table.
Option D: Streams are exactly-once, so the projection stays correct.

Question: In DynamoDB, strongly consistent reads cost more and still do not make a GSI or a default global-table replica 'the truth everywhere'. The honest contract is:
Option A: Strong reads lock all GSIs

Option D: A strong GetItem is a read of that region's partition leader, not a global lock; GSIs stay eventually consistent, and default (MREC) global tables are async unless you chose MRSC

Question: In DynamoDB, time-series data with PK = today's date concentrates today's writes. A better key shape is:

Question: In DynamoDB, you are asked to 'just add an index' for an unplanned access pattern. What do you check first?

Question: In DynamoDB, you are designing for a 10× Prime-Day-like spike on a few product keys. Adaptive capacity and on-demand help, but what still requires modeling work?

Question: In Java, a thread writes several fields, then publishes the object by storing it into a concurrent queue. Another thread takes it. Why can this be correct without volatile on each field?

Question: In Java, flight Recorder (or a sampling profiler) shows a hot lock, but the code looks wait-free. What should you check before rewriting the algorithm?

Question: In Java, time-to-safepoint is high: a thread is in a tight loop or JNI without poll points. What does the process look like?

Question: In Java, you grow a heap from 30 GB to 40 GB and RSS jumps more than the extra 10 GB, with worse GC. What geometry did you likely just lose?

Question: You adopt virtual threads for a servlet app, but a hot path still does `synchronized (mutex) { jdbc.call(); }`. Even if pinning is improved on newer JDKs, what remains the staff-level problem?

Question: You copy a thread-pool pattern that caches a JDBC Connection in a ThreadLocal onto Java 21+ virtual threads (potentially millions). What breaks?

Question: In Kubernetes, rollingUpdate maxUnavailable: 1 on a StatefulSet of 5 databases, each with a PVC. Why is this not the same as a Deployment surge?

Question: In Kubernetes, you mark a Deployment progressDeadlineSeconds too low while image pulls are slow. Interaction with rolling update?

Question: In Kubernetes, you need disruption-safe cluster autoscaler + PDB + HPA. Which invariant is the one that actually allows a node to go away?

Question: In Kubernetes, you need zonal disruption (one AZ down) to leave the service up. PDB minAvailable=80% and 3 replicas. Why is that a false SLO?

Question: In Kubernetes, you set a liveness exec probe that deadlocks on the same global lock as the request path. Failure mode?

Question: A hot row (counter) is updated by many sessions. InnoDB exhibits severe mutex/lock waits despite a tiny row. Which design actually scales?
Option A: Switching binlog to STATEMENT so updates merge
Option B: Raising the buffer pool so row locks are not taken
Option C: Sharding the counter into many rows or moving increments to a log/queue so clustered-record lock contention is spread

Question: A huge InnoDB table must be resharded because the PK is a hot increment and one instance is CPU-bound. What is the scaling move that actually works?

Question: Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster vs a classic async replica + orchestrated failover. You need to write in two regions. What is the honest limitation?

Option B: Async replication cannot be used for reads.

Option D: Group Replication gives you active-active multi-region writes with no conflict rules.

Question: In MySQL, a descending scan of a secondary index plus clustered lookups causes 'random' primary-key I/O. How does a covering index or clustering change the shape?
Option A: Buffer pool prefetch only works on UUID keys
Option B: Gap locks force sequential PK access regardless of index
Option C: Covering avoids PK jumps; alternatively, designing the clustered key to match the access order turns random lookups into range reads
Option D: InnoDB always stores secondary indexes in PK order

Question: In MySQL, a finance ledger requires 'read your writes' and audit of who changed a row. Why is a read replica the wrong place for the audit query immediately after commit?
Option A: Audit must be done in the application memory only.
Option B: Replicas have stronger isolation than the primary.
Option C: Async apply means the replica may not have the row; the audit source of truth is the primary (or a commit-wait / session-consistent mechanism).
Option D: Binlog does not contain UPDATEs.

Question: In MySQL, a generated column stored in the clustered index is used to index JSON. Why can this still be a write-amplification trap?
Option A: Generated columns cannot be part of a secondary index
Option B: JSON updates skip redo logging when generated columns exist
Option C: Gap locks are taken on every JSON path globally
Option D: Every base-column update rewrites the clustered row and maintains the generated value plus any indexes on it, inflating undo and binlog images

Question: In MySQL, a multi-table UPDATE with a join under RR locks more gaps than the business key suggests. What planner/lock interaction is involved?
Option A: The chosen index and scan direction determine next-key lock ranges, including extra gaps if the access path is not a precise unique PK lookup
Option B: Joins always take a global metadata lock instead of row locks
Option C: RR disables index condition pushdown so locks cover the table
Option D: Binlog row events take the locks on the replica only

Question: In MySQL, a point-in-time restore uses binlog + a backup taken with a snapshot. Restored data has extra or missing rows around the snapshot LSN. What was likely misaligned?
Option A: Covering indexes cannot be recovered from binlog
Option B: READ COMMITTED backups skip the redo log
Option C: The backup's InnoDB LSN / GTID set was not consistent with the binlog position applied, so recovery replayed the wrong range of row events
Option D: Gap locks from the snapshot were not restored

Question: In MySQL, crash recovery after a huge dirty buffer pool is slow even with a healthy redo log. Which setting tension is this?
Option A: A large buffer pool with infrequent checkpoints / large max redo means more redo to apply and more dirty pages to flush on recovery
Option B: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1 disables recovery
Option C: Row-based binlog replaces InnoDB redo, so recovery replays the binlog only
Option D: Gap locks must be rebuilt from the binary log before the server opens

Question: In MySQL, during online rebuild DDL, concurrent DML is logged to an online log. What failure mode appears if that log overflows or the table is extremely hot?
Option A: InnoDB silently drops DML that occurred during DDL
Option B: The replica applies DDL without the concurrent DML
Option C: Gap locks are converted to checksums in the online log
Option D: The ALTER fails or throttles; concurrent writes either abort the DDL or stall until the sort/apply of DML can catch up

Question: In MySQL, group Replication / a source-replica topology hits flow control because one replica's applier is slower. What is the real availability trade-off?
Option A: The buffer pool is automatically resized to zero on slow members
Option B: The source throttles or the lagging member is expelled; you choose between write stalls and weaker durability/consistency of the set
Option C: Flow control only affects SELECT on the source
Option D: InnoDB stops taking gap locks during flow control

Question: In MySQL, temp tables in a transaction with binlog ROW and a rollback. Why can disk and replication still surprise you?
Option A: Gap locks on temp tables are copied to the replica
Option B: Some temp-table patterns still write row events or consume undo/ibtmp; rollback does not shrink files, and mixed temp usage can desync replicas if logged incorrectly
Option C: Temporary tables are always replicated as CREATE TABLE on disk
Option D: Rollback of temp tables requires a full clustered rebuild of user tables

Question: In MySQL, you enable binlog_row_image = FULL for audit, then switch to MINIMAL to cut WAL-like binlog volume. What replica/trigger failure can MINIMAL cause?
Option A: Covering indexes become invalid on replicas
Option B: Replicas, row-based triggers, or tools that need unchanged columns cannot reconstruct the full before image
Option C: MINIMAL disables crash recovery in InnoDB
Option D: Gap locks are omitted from redo

Question: In MySQL, you observe replication lag that grows only when the primary does bulk LOAD. Row-based replication is on. Why can the replica still fall over?
Option A: Binlog compresses bulk loads to one page the replica cannot unpack.
Option B: The replica must take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on every table.
Option C: Row-based events for huge writes apply row-by-row on the replica, often without the primary's bulk optimizations.
Option D: Replicas ignore LOAD DATA.

Question: In MySQL, you set replica_preserve_commit_order = ON with parallel workers. Throughput drops vs unordered apply. Why is that the correct default for many systems?
Option A: It is required for covering indexes to work
Option B: It prevents gap locks on the source
Option C: Readers and cascading replicas observe the same commit order as the source, avoiding anomalies that cheaper parallel apply would allow
Option D: Commit order preservation disables the redo log on the replica

Question: In MySQL, you split a hotspot table by hash of tenant_id into multiple tables to reduce clustered-page contention. Which cost did you just accept?
Option A: The buffer pool cannot cache more than one shard

Option C: InnoDB can no longer use secondary indexes
Option D: Gap locks disappear because hash tables have no order

Question: InnoDB RR phantom protection uses next-key locks, but a SELECT without FOR UPDATE uses MVCC snapshots. A read-then-write transaction still commits a write skew. Why is RR not SERIALIZABLE here?

Option C: The binary log serializes all snapshot reads

Question: You consider SERIALIZABLE in InnoDB to kill write-skew. What operational price shows up under high read concurrency?

Option B: SERIALIZABLE disables the buffer pool for reads

Question: In PostgreSQL, a BRIN index is chosen for a time-series table that is updated in the middle of the key range. Why does BRIN degrade?

Question: In PostgreSQL, a connection pooler in session mode plus thousands of idle-in-transaction sessions. Memory on the database host climbs. Why is this worse than idle (not in transaction)?

Question: In PostgreSQL, a multi-master-like design uses logical replication with conflict avoidance by partitioning key ranges per node. An UPDATE moves a row across ranges. What breaks?

Question: In PostgreSQL, a multi-tenant SaaS puts all tenants in one cluster. One tenant runs analytical queries that blow up work_mem and temp files. What isolation strategy actually protects neighbors?

Option D: Disable TTL so Redis becomes source of truth

Question: In Redis, streams with consumer groups beat a naive list queue when:
Option A: You need cluster-wide ACID
Option B: You need pending entries, acknowledgements, and replay after a worker crash — still not a durable business ledger by itself
Option C: You need strongly consistent GSIs
Option D: You want eviction to delete jobs first

Question: In Redis, why can pipelining + Cluster be wrong if you blindly batch keys?
Option A: Pipelines disable eviction mid-batch as a transaction
Option B: Pipelines cannot send SET
Option C: A pipeline is still per-node; mixed slots must be split by slot or you get CROSSSLOT / extra hops
Option D: Pipelines force RDB

Question: In Redis, you need a distributed lock. Someone uses SET NX without expiry, or with expiry but no fencing token. What bug remains?
Option A: Expiry is unnecessary if clients are in the same VPC.
Option B: None; NX is a correct lock.
Option C: A lock can be held forever, or expire while work continues and a second worker runs — without fencing, both sides mutate the resource.
Option D: Redis locks are linearizable if you use WAIT.

Question: Redis is used as a session store. A replica is promoted after async replication lag. What did users just lose, and what is the staff fix?
Option A: Nothing; promotion waits for replicas.
Option B: Recent sessions/writes that never made the replica; either accept RPO, use WAIT/sync replication (latency), or don't put irreplaceable sessions only in Redis.
Option C: AOF on the new primary contains the old primary's unsent writes automatically.
Option D: Clients reconnect and Redis heals sessions from S3.

Question: Stampede plus a single-threaded Redis plus a slow DB fill is a cascade. A robust refill looks like:
Option A: TTL=0 on every key
Option B: One owner refills, others wait or serve stale; optionally jitter TTLs; never let N app servers all reconstruct the same key
Option C: Flushall on miss
Option D: Disable pipelining during refill

Question: Why still persist a write to Postgres (or similar) when Redis already SET it?
Option A: AOF cannot store the same string
Option B: Postgres is faster
Option C: Redis may evict, lose a replica, or replay an older RDB; the database is the source of truth, Redis is a copy
Option D: Cluster slots require SQL

Question: You observe p99 spikes every N minutes with no app deploy. A likely Redis cause is:
Option A: Cluster slots wrapping at 16384
Option B: Fork-based persistence, large expiry storms, or big-key commands — all block or stall the same thread
Option C: Eventually consistent reads
Option D: On-demand memory billing

Question: A Spring Boot app puts userId on every Micrometer timer. After a traffic spike, Prometheus/memory dies. What happened?
Option A: Micrometer drops tags longer than three characters.
Option B: Timers cannot have tags, so this configuration is rejected at startup.
Option C: High-cardinality tags explode time series. Bound tags to a small enum (route, status, instance), never unbounded IDs.
Option D: Prometheus automatically rolls up userId into a histogram.

Question: A Spring MVC (servlet) app uses WebClient.block() on the request thread for every downstream call. What did you not buy?
Option A: You still occupy a servlet thread for the whole wait; WebClient only helps if the pipeline is actually non-blocking. A pooled RestClient may be simpler and as fast.
Option B: block() migrates the work to Netty event loops and frees Tomcat.
Option C: WebClient.block is illegal in MVC and will not compile.
Option D: You bought full reactive backpressure end-to-end.

Question: A custom OncePerRequestFilter authenticates after Spring Security's authorization filter because you registered it as a plain @Component Filter. What is the failure?
Option A: Security filter chain order is explicit; a late filter can run after the decision or sit outside the chain. Register it in the SecurityFilterChain at the right position.
Option B: @Component filters always run first, before Spring Security.
Option C: Authorization does not use filters in Boot 3.
Option D: Filter order is random and usually fine in Boot 3.

Question: A payment service must not lose 'charge then record' if the process dies after HTTP 200 from Stripe. What Spring-centric pattern actually works?
Option A: @Async so the charge happens after response.
Option B: XA with Stripe's JDBC driver.
Option C: @Transactional around the Stripe SDK call.
Option D: Idempotency key + outbox (record intent, commit, then charge/publish) so crash recovery can finish the work without double-charge.

Question: In Spring Boot, a @KafkaListener writes to the DB then relies on auto-commit of the offset. Auto-commit is on, DB commit is separate. What lost-update/duplicate class is this?
Option A: Auto-commit waits for @Transactional to finish.
Option B: Kafka and the DB share a transaction by default in Spring.
Option C: At-least-once delivery: you can process twice or lose the ack. Use idempotent writes and commit the offset after DB commit (or a transaction manager that covers both).
Option D: Kafka listeners are exactly-once if the topic has one partition.

Question: In Spring Boot, a platform team enables /actuator/refresh to change secrets in place. Why do staff teams often prefer immutable deploys instead?
Option A: Half-applied config, stale singletons, and secret-in-memory linger; a new process with a new config artifact is a known state.
Option B: Immutable deploys cannot change env vars at all.
Option C: /refresh encrypts all beans, so it is strictly safer than a restart.
Option D: Refresh always restarts the JVM cleanly, which is slower than a rolling deploy.

Question: In Spring Boot, two Boot services share a database and Hibernate entities. Why do staff platform teams fight this?
Option A: Connection pools cannot be sized per service.
Option B: Hibernate cannot map the same table twice in the world.
Option C: You coupled deployability and schemas: migrations, locks, and incompatible entity changes become a distributed monolith. Split data ownership.
Option D: Spring forbids two apps on one JDBC URL.

Question: In Spring Boot, you enable virtual threads in Boot 3.2+ but keep a 200-thread Tomcat pool and an @Async executor of 500 platform threads 'for safety'. What did you misunderstand?
Option A: Virtual threads are meant to replace giant platform pools on blocking I/O. Bound the real scarce resource (JDBC pool, downstream connections), not thread count; two huge platform pools fight the model.
Option B: Virtual threads cannot run on servlet stacks, so the Tomcat pool is still the only concurrency knob.
Option C: @Async always uses virtual threads once the property is set, so the executor size is ignored.
Option D: Virtual threads require even larger platform pools so carriers never starve.

Question: In Spring Boot, you inherited a monolith Boot app that starts a full context for every integration test. CI is 40 minutes. What is the staff testing strategy?
Option A: Disable tests in CI to restore speed.
Option B: Replace JUnit with main() methods.
Option C: Only @SpringBootTest; slicing hides bugs.
Option D: Slice tests for web/data, testcontainers for a few contract tests, and a small number of full-context smoke tests — not a full boot per method.

Question: Kubernetes SIGTERM hits a Spring Boot app with in-flight 30s requests and server.shutdown is immediate (or an old default). What happens?
Option A: The process dies mid-request unless graceful shutdown plus a preStop sleep cover in-flight work inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Option B: kubelet waits forever for HTTP to drain.
Option C: Actuator liveness extends the grace period automatically.
Option D: Spring always waits for in-flight requests regardless of that property.

Question: Spring Retry retries a 502 from a downstream on a write that is not idempotent. What do you actually cause?
Option A: Spring Retry deduplicates by URL automatically.
Option B: 502 is a read-only signal; Spring will not retry writes.
Option C: Retries are always safe for HTTP because 502 means the write never happened.
Option D: Duplicate side effects (double charge, double email) unless the callee is idempotent. Retry budgets belong on idempotent reads or with idempotency keys.

Question: Two tenants share one Spring Boot app and one Hibernate EntityManager. You forget the tenant-id predicate on a query. What is the incident?
Option A: Cross-tenant data leak. Tenant isolation must be in every query (filter, discriminator, or separate schema/DB) and tested; a missing WHERE is a security bug.
Option B: Spring Security tenancy is implied by the JWT, so queries cannot leak.
Option C: One EntityManager cannot see two tenants' rows by construction.
Option D: Hibernate adds tenant filters automatically to native SQL.

Question: You need to expand-contract a NOT NULL column while doing a rolling Spring Boot deploy. Why is 'add NOT NULL with default in the same release as the readers' dangerous?
Option A: NOT NULL is ignored until the next restart, so the same release is always safe.
Option B: Flyway cannot add columns during a rolling deploy.
Option C: Old instances may write without the new column/code path; mixed versions plus a blocking rewrite can lock the table. Expand (nullable/backfill) then contract after the fleet is new.
Option D: Rolling deploys always take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE in Hibernate.
